## Design

### 2026-10-14 – Onshape Marble Run Session: Base Plate, Straight Blocks, Curves, Pillars, and Ramps

**5h**

Onshape Marble Run Session: Base Plate, Straight Blocks, Curves, Pillars, and Ramps

Today Objective
My main goal today was to learn how the tools work in Onshape and build out every single core piece of my modular marble run step by step, making sure every dimension matched our grid system so I could test assembling a full multi level tower.

What I Did Today
I spent five hours figuring out the software, because I really struggled with learning how all the CAD tools worked. I started out with the base plate, which gave me a solid grid foundation packed with socket holes for everything else to plug into. After that, I built the normal straight block, which measures 40 mm by 40 mm by 20 mm, and has a little 8 mm snap peg on the bottom, plus an 18 mm wide track channel carved into the top.

Next up was the ninety degree curve piece on a 40 mm by 40 mm by 20 mm block, where I used arcs to map out a smooth turning track. Following the curve, I designed the support pillar block, which stands 40 mm tall, featuring an 8 mm peg on the bottom and an 8.2 mm socket on top for stacking. Then I tackled the long ramp piece, which measures 80 mm by 40 mm by 40 mm to span two grid units and bridge vertical heights.

Once all the individual parts were modeled, I jumped into an assembly studio to start testing how everything fits together by inserting the base plate, pillars, tiles, and ramps, and using fastened mates and the triad tool to snap them into place.

Mistakes I Ran Into and How I Fixed Them
I ran into several tricky spots during the session because I was still getting used to the software. On the ninety degree curve, my track lines looked way too sharp and jagged instead of flowing smoothly, which I fixed by using the three point arc tool and carving out an 18 mm channel with an 8.8 mm fillet.

I also struggled heavily with the 80 mm ramp design, because I kept messing up the slope height until I realized the block needed to start at 40 mm high and drop down precisely to 20 mm using the dimension tool, so it would actually line up nicely with my other blocks.

Later, when I tried putting everything together in the assembly workspace, I realized I forgot to add the bottom pegs to some of my duplicated parts, so I had to bounce back into the part studios to sketch an 8 mm circle and extrude it by 4.8 mm. I also struggled a bit with getting the pieces flipped and rotated right using the assembly mate flipping buttons and the triad tool before everything finally clicked into place.

Wrap Up
With all the foundational blocks, straight tiles, ninety degree curves, 40 mm pillars, and 80 mm long ramps built and properly dimensioned, the modular marble run component library is shaping up nicely and ready for full scale tower building despite the steep learning curve.

Total time spent: 5 hours

### 2026-10-15 – Extended Drop Hole Tile Journal

**5h**

Extended Drop Hole Tile Journal
I wanted a piece that gives the marble a bit more runway before dropping through to a lower level, so I built an 80 by 40 by 20 mm tile. I started with a center point rectangle sketch, extruded it up 20 mm, and carved an 18 mm track along the top deck. Towards the far end, I placed a center circle drop hole and added a slight chamfer around the top rim to act like a gentle funnel. Flipping it over, I added two bottom pegs spaced 40 mm apart so it snaps right onto the grid.

Y-Split Junction Tile Journal
To add some unpredictability to the marble run, I created a 40 by 40 by 20 mm splitter block. I started with a standard extruded base and sketched a straight 18 mm channel entering from one side. Midway through the block, I split the sketch into two diagonal exit paths using three point arcs. After sweeping the remove paths and filleting the bottom corners with an 8.8 mm radius, the marble can now randomly choose between two different routes as it rolls through.

Catch Basin End Stop Block Journal
Every good layout needs a solid terminal piece to keep marbles from bouncing off the table, so I designed a dedicated catch basin. I extruded a standard 40 by 40 by 20 mm block and sketched an 18 mm entry channel that stops short near the center. Using a circular pocket extrude remove, I created a recessed landing cup with a smooth filleted bowl. The marble rolls in, hits the back wall, drops into the pocket, and safely stays put.

Double S-Curve Wiggle Tile Journal
To give the track a fun snake like motion, I designed an extended 160 by 40 by 20 mm block spanning four grid units. I drew three vertical construction lines to set up four 40 by 40 mm quadrants, then placed five tangent points across the block. Connecting them with four 3-point arcs set to a 22.5 mm radius created a super smooth wiggle line. I swept an 18 mm track along the path, applied an 8.8 mm fillet to the bottom edges using tangent propagation, and extruded four bottom snap pegs.

Vortex Funnel Tile Journal
For the ultimate hero piece, I created a huge 120 by 120 by 20 mm tile that spans a 3 by 3 grid. I extruded the large square base and sketched an 110 mm outer rim circle with an 18 mm drop hole right in the center. I used an extrude remove with a 15 degree draft angle to carve out a massive sloped funnel bowl. After cutting a tangent entry track on one side so the marble enters along the wall and swirls around, I extruded eight bottom pegs around the outer grid positions, leaving the center column completely open for the marble to fall through.

### 2026-10-18 – Pieces 11–13

**3h**

Pieces 11–13
vortex
what it does: spirals the marble around a big funnel before dropping it down to the lower level.

how it was made: drawn on an 80x80mm double grid footprint with a centered drop hole for 16mm marbles. used a smooth curved revolved profile so the marble spins around without flying off the edge.

notes: great timing delay piece to slow down the marble before the final run.

catch basin
what it does: sits at the very end of the track to stop the marble so it doesn't roll off your desk or floor.

how it was made: 40x40mm single grid footprint with a dished-out bowl and a back wall stopper.

notes: angled slightly backward so when high-speed marbles hit the back, they drop right into the dish instead of bouncing out.

marble
what it does: the 16mm rolling sphere used to run through all the tracks.

how it was made: revolved a 16mm semi-circle profile 360 degrees to create a perfect reference sphere.

notes: super useful in onshape to check clearances across track channels, drop holes, and vortex drains before printing.
